title: Design a Chat Service
brief: People send short messages to friends and groups over a live connection. Every message must reach the other side in the order it was sent, be kept in the conversation history, and, if a recipient is offline, trigger a push notification through an outside provider. Evenings are much busier than the rest of the day.
constraints: Accepting a message must take under 150 ms
About 5,000 messages per second at peak, and three times that on a busy evening
Messages in one conversation are delivered in the order they were sent
Every message is kept in the conversation history
About 3 in 10 recipients are offline and get a push notification from an external provider
About 5 billion messages are stored, and people scroll back through long conversations

capabilities.label: Accept a message
capabilities.hint: Hold the live connection and accept what the user sends

capabilities.label: Deliver in order
capabilities.hint: Hand each message to its recipients, in the order the sender sent them

capabilities.label: Save the history
capabilities.hint: Store every message so the conversation can be read later

capabilities.label: Push to offline devices
capabilities.hint: Ask the push provider to notify recipients who are not connected

queries.label: Load a page of a conversation, newest first

scenarios.title: Typical peak
scenarios.description: Steady messaging at the usual peak.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Which parts of sending a message must finish before you acknowledge it, and which can happen after?
scenarios.debrief: The chat server only accepts and appends. Delivery, history and push all happen after the acknowledgement.

scenarios.title: Busy evening (3x)
scenarios.description: Evening traffic triples the message rate.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: What gives first when the rate triples, and how do you add capacity without breaking per-conversation order?
scenarios.debrief: Partitions spread conversations across consumers, and autoscaling widens the workers for the busy evening.

scenarios.title: Delivery workers fail
scenarios.description: Whatever runs delivery loses an instance.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: A delivery worker dies in the middle of a conversation. How do you avoid losing or reordering messages?
scenarios.debrief: Another delivery worker takes over the partition and continues from its last position, so order is kept.

scenarios.title: Push provider outage
scenarios.description: The external push provider stops answering.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: You cannot control the push provider. What happens to messages and to offline users when it is down?
scenarios.debrief: Push is an optional consumer. When the provider is down, messages are still delivered and stored.

requirements.text: Messages are accepted within the latency target at peak
The busy evening passes without losing messages
Messages travel through a Stream, so order is kept per conversation
Messaging keeps working when the push provider is down
The design explains how order is kept per conversation, and what the partition key is
Every query is answered through a key or an index, never by reading a whole table

rubric: Messages are appended to a Stream keyed by conversation, so each conversation is ordered while different conversations spread across partitions.
Acknowledging a message does not wait for delivery, history or push; those are separate consumers of the stream.
History uses a store suited to heavy appends (key-value or document), not a single relational primary.
Push is optional and isolated: a provider outage costs notifications, not messages.
Delivery workers can fail without reordering or dropping messages (offsets, idempotent handling).

reference.summary: Acknowledge fast, put every message on a stream keyed by conversation, and let separate consumers deliver, store and push.
design: User, then a Load Balancer, then a WebSocket Server (2 replicas) running 'Accept a message'.
It appends each message to a Stream (4 partitions, keyed by conversation, 24 hour retention) asynchronously.

Three consumers read the stream: Workers for 'Deliver in order', Workers for 'Save the history' into a key-value Database, and Workers for 'Push to offline devices' that call a Third-party API set to Email / SMS.
tradeoffs: A Stream (not a Queue) keeps order per conversation and lets new consumers replay, at a higher cost than a plain queue.
A key-value store handles heavy appends cheaply but gives up joins and multi-row transactions.
